analysis.one_liner: Limits credit lines for college students and requires parents to approve credit limit increases.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill protecting college students from credit card overspending gathered 58 cosponsors but never got a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal lending law so credit card companies could not give full-time college students unlimited credit. Unless a parent or guardian agreed to share responsibility for the debt, a student's credit limit would be capped based on their income, and parents would have to approve in writing any raise to a limit they were on the hook for. It would also bar companies from issuing a second card to a student with no income who already had one, and require that the fine print in card offers be printed in type at least as large as the biggest type in the ad.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time college students and their parents. Students would be protected from building up large credit card balances on cards marketed to them on campus, and parents who co-sign would no longer face surprise limit increases. Disclosure in ads would be easier to read.

how_it_helps.text: Caps a student's total credit line at the greater of 20% of their annual gross income or $500 per year since the account opened, up to $2,000, unless a parent or guardian takes joint responsibility for the debt [S3].
Bars creditors from raising the credit limit on any card a parent or guardian co-signed without that parent's written approval, while the student is still a traditional-aged college student [S3].
Prohibits issuing any credit card to a full-time college student who has no annual income and already holds another credit card account [S3].

Requires the legally required disclosures in card applications and solicitations to appear in type at least as large as the largest type in the document, so the disclosure cannot be buried in fine print [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose the ability to extend large credit lines to college students with little or no income and to raise limits without a co-signing parent's approval.

drawbacks.text: The formula caps would also limit credit for students who genuinely manage small credit lines responsibly, since access would depend on past income or a parent co-signing rather than the student's actual ability to repay [S3].
Some students without parental support would find it harder to build a credit history or cover emergency costs, because the alternative to a parent's joint liability is a much lower cap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a specific, well-documented problem: cards marketed to students who cannot legally drink being extended thousands of dollars in credit. The cost is that some financially capable students would face lower limits or need a parent's signature. On balance the protections are modest and targeted, though the income-based formula is a blunt instrument that does not distinguish a student who can repay from one who cannot.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its consumer credit subcommittee for two years without ever getting a vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Representative Louise Slaughter of New York introduced the College Student Credit Card Protection Act on January 3, 2001, the first day of the 107th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on January 3, 2001, and on March 2, 2001 was sent to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill had 58 cosponsors, 48 of 208 House Democrats, 9 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers are better off: the restrictions were never enacted, so issuers kept the ability to market cards to students and extend them credit based on factors other than income. Students and parents who would have gained the protections got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — 48 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and the chamber's one Independent cosponsored — but no vote was ever taken, so the party split never got tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and card companies)
industries.note: The bill would cap the credit they could extend to traditional-aged college students, require parental approval for limit increases on co-signed cards, and bar issuing second cards to income-less students. Their interest in opposing ran directly against the students and parents the bill protected.

Colleges define who counts as a traditional-aged student, which determines who the protections cover, and campus card marketing to students would be constrained. Students and parents would gain the most.
